key_results: DSP is framed as the mathematics, algorithms, and techniques applied after real-world sensory signals are digitized. Its transferable core sits amid overlapping communication theory, numerical analysis, probability/statistics, analog processing, electronics, and decision theory rather than forming a sharply isolated field. [Chapter 1, The Roots of DSP and Fig. 1-2]

The same primitives recur across applications: multiplexing and compression in telecommunications, filtering and artificial reverberation in audio, matched pulse detection in radar/sonar, reflection analysis in seismology, and enhancement/reconstruction/compression in imaging. [Chapter 1, Telecommunications through Image Processing]

For a finite signal, the mean is the sample average; the unbiased sample variance divides the squared-deviation sum by N−1, and standard deviation is its square root. Standard deviation describes the AC fluctuation, whereas RMS includes both AC and DC and equals standard deviation only for zero-mean signals. [Chapter 2, Mean and Standard Deviation, Eqs. 2-1–2-2]

Running statistics need retain only N, the running sum, and the running sum of squares; mean and variance can be recomputed without storing or rescanning all samples. This form improves computational efficiency, though modern implementations should still consider numerical stability. [Chapter 2, Mean and Standard Deviation, Eq. 2-3 and Table 2-2]

Statistics describe an acquired finite record; probability describes the process that generated it. The typical error of a sample-mean estimate is σ/√N, and the Strong Law of Large Numbers guarantees convergence of the estimated mean as N grows. [Chapter 2, Signal versus Underlying Process, Eq. 2-4]

A histogram counts observed discrete values and sums to N; a probability mass function assigns discrete probabilities and sums to one; a probability density function applies to a continuous variable and has unit area. Binning makes histogram methods workable for large-valued or floating-point data. [Chapter 2, The Histogram, PMF and PDF, Eqs. 2-5–2-7, Figs. 2-4–2-7]

For a normal distribution, about 68%, 95%, and 99.75% of samples lie within ±1σ, ±2σ, and ±3σ. Its rapidly decaying tails explain why Gaussian random signals appear to have a practical peak-to-peak span of roughly 6–8σ even though they are theoretically unbounded. [Chapter 2, The Normal Distribution, Figs. 2-8–2-9]

The Central Limit Theorem explains why summing independent random contributions tends toward a Gaussian even when the component distributions are not Gaussian. A simple generator sums twelve uniform random variables, subtracts six, and then scales/shifts to the desired σ and mean. [Chapter 2, Digital Noise Generation, Fig. 2-10]

Precision is governed by random variation and can improve through averaging; accuracy is governed by systematic/calibration error and cannot. The diagnostic questions are whether averaging helps (precision) and whether calibration helps (accuracy). [Chapter 2, Precision and Accuracy]

Quantization is usually modeled as additive uniform noise between ±1/2 LSB, with zero mean and standard deviation 1/√12≈0.29 LSB. Independent analog and quantization noise combine by adding variances, so converter bit depth should be chosen relative to the noise already present and the noise the application can tolerate. [Chapter 3, Quantization, Fig. 3-1]

The additive-noise model fails for slowly varying or nearly constant inputs whose quantization error becomes signal-correlated. Dither deliberately adds noise so repeated samples toggle among adjacent codes; their average can then estimate sub-LSB signal levels—an explicit case where adding noise reveals information. [Chapter 3, Quantization, Figs. 3-2–3-3]

The sampling theorem requires an analog signal contain no components above half the sampling rate for unique reconstruction. Sampling replicates the analog spectrum at integer multiples of f_s; aliasing occurs when those replicas overlap, irreversibly merging frequencies. [Chapter 3, The Sampling Theorem, Figs. 3-4–3-5]

A practical DAC performs a zero-order hold rather than emitting ideal impulses. The hold multiplies the spectrum by sinc(f/f_s), causing about 36% high-frequency compensation at f_s/2 in an ideal reconstruction filter in addition to removal of spectral images above Nyquist. [Chapter 3, Digital-to-Analog Conversion, Eq. 3-1 and Fig. 3-6]

Analog and digital signals are constrained by the same information limits: amplitude resolution is limited by noise/quantization, and time resolution by bandwidth/sampling. A bandlimited analog signal and its properly sampled digital representation contain the same information; continuity does not imply infinite resolution. [Chapter 3, Digital-to-Analog Conversion]

Chebyshev, Butterworth, and Bessel analog filters optimize different objectives: transition sharpness, passband flatness, and step response respectively. Filter choice should follow how information is encoded—frequency-domain signals favor sharp rejection, while time-domain waveform shape favors Bessel-like transient fidelity. [Chapter 3, Analog Filters for Data Conversion and Selecting the Antialias Filter, Table 3-2]

For time-domain-encoded data, an aggressive antialias filter can destroy the feature being measured even while satisfying the sampling theorem. A Bessel filter trades gentle edge rounding for high-frequency rejection; no filter preserves sample values but leaves aliased interference and loses sub-sample timing cues. [Chapter 3, Selecting the Antialias Filter, Fig. 3-15]

Multirate conversion moves demanding filtering into software: sample fast behind a simple analog filter, digitally low-pass, then decimate; reverse with zero insertion, digital low-pass interpolation, DAC, and a simple reconstruction network. The chapter's voice example converts between 64 kHz and 8 kHz by factors of eight. [Chapter 3, Multirate Data Conversion]

Delta modulation encodes the slope of an input in the relative density of ones and zeros and is limited by the coupled choices of step size, slew rate, and data rate. Delta-sigma instead makes bit density track signal level; digital low-pass filtering and decimation turn its oversampled one-bit stream into conventional multibit samples. [Chapter 3, Single-Bit Data Conversion, Figs. 3-16–3-19]

A 16-bit two's-complement integer spans −32,768 to 32,767. IEEE single precision uses a sign bit, 8-bit biased exponent, and 23 stored fraction bits (with an implicit leading one); its relative spacing is about one part in 8–17 million, unlike the constant unit spacing of fixed point. [Chapter 4, Fixed Point through Number Precision, Figs. 4-1–4-3]

Roundoff can accumulate randomly as √K or coherently as K after K operations; because the sign pattern is algorithm-dependent and difficult to predict, the text recommends budgeting for additive worst-case accumulation. Integer counters avoid this class of drift entirely. [Chapter 4, Number Precision, Fig. 4-4 and Table 4-2]

Single-precision floating point exactly represents every integer through ±2²⁴≈±16.8 million. Powers-of-two fractions also have exact binary representations, whereas decimal increments such as 0.01 generally do not; loop control should therefore use integer indices. [Chapter 4, Number Precision]

Execution speed depends as much on data movement and architecture as arithmetic: cache reduces main-memory stalls, Harvard architectures fetch program and data simultaneously, pipelines overlap successive operations, and DSP processors provide dedicated multiply-accumulate hardware. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Hardware, Fig. 4-5]

A practical optimization hierarchy is to choose integer arithmetic when its range suffices, avoid repeated transcendental functions, precompute finite-domain functions in lookup tables, and benchmark the actual platform—especially I/O and graphics paths. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Programming Tips]

A DSP system is linear when it satisfies homogeneity and additivity; shift invariance is a separate property but is conventionally assumed in most DSP uses of 'linear system.' Shift invariance means a shifted input produces only the identical shift in the output. [Chapter 5, Requirements for Linearity, Figs. 5-2–5-4]

Sinusoidal fidelity is the defining intuition behind frequency response: a sinusoid passed through an LTI system remains a sinusoid at exactly the same frequency, changing only amplitude and phase. No other waveform has this universal eigenfunction property. [Chapter 5, Static Linearity and Sinusoidal Fidelity]

Superposition is the foundational strategy of DSP: decompose a complicated input into additive components, process each through the linear system, and synthesize the output components. The result equals processing the original signal directly. [Chapter 5, Superposition: the Foundation of DSP, Fig. 5-11]

Impulse decomposition leads to convolution; Fourier decomposition leads to spectral analysis; step, even/odd, and interlaced decompositions expose other useful structures. Interlaced decomposition is the recursive split underlying FFT speedups. [Chapter 5, Common Decompositions, Figs. 5-12–5-16]

Nonlinear systems are commonly handled by ignoring small nonlinearities, restricting operation to a small-signal approximately linear region, or applying a linearizing transform. Logarithms, for example, turn multiplication into addition in homomorphic processing. [Chapter 5, Alternatives to Linearity]

The impulse response completely characterizes an LTI system because an arbitrary input is a sum of shifted, scaled impulses. Convolution performs the corresponding sum of shifted, scaled impulse responses to produce the output. [Chapter 6, The Delta Function and Impulse Response through The Input-Side Algorithm]

For an N-sample input and M-sample impulse response, linear convolution has N+M−1 samples and obeys y[i]=Σ_{j=0}^{M−1}h[j]x[i−j], with undefined input samples treated as zero. The first and last M−1 outputs are boundary transients based on incomplete support. [Chapter 6, The Output-Side Algorithm, Eq. 6-1 and Fig. 6-10]

Input-side convolution distributes each input sample into a shifted/scaled impulse response; output-side convolution flips the impulse response and computes each output as a dot product. They are exactly the same operation and provide complementary implementation intuitions. [Chapter 6, The Input-Side Algorithm through The Sum of Weighted Inputs]

Convolving with a delta leaves a signal unchanged; scaled or shifted deltas implement gain and delay, and a sum of deltas implements echoes. First difference h=[1,−1] and running sum are discrete analogues of differentiation and integration and are inverse operations. [Chapter 7, Common Impulse Responses, Eqs. 7-1–7-5]

Convolution is commutative, associative, and distributive. Thus cascaded LTI systems may be reordered and replaced by convolution of their impulse responses, while parallel systems with summed outputs may be replaced by the sum of their impulse responses. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Eqs. 7-6–7-8]

Repeated self-convolution of a pulse converges rapidly toward a Gaussian; its width σ grows by the square root of the convolution count. This is the convolutional form of the Central Limit Theorem. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Fig. 7-12]

Cross-correlation measures similarity versus relative shift and peaks where a known target aligns with a received record. It equals convolution after reversing one operand and is the optimal linear detector of a known waveform in additive white noise—the matched-filter result. [Chapter 7, Correlation, Figs. 7-13–7-14]

Direct convolution costs N×M multiply-accumulates. The text uses this concrete cost to motivate short kernels, DSP hardware, and FFT convolution, which gives the identical result and can be hundreds of times faster for long records. [Chapter 7, Speed]

The real DFT represents an N-sample real record by N/2+1 cosine coefficients and N/2+1 sine coefficients, with special DC and Nyquist endpoint scaling; equivalently, polar form uses N/2+1 magnitudes and phases. Its basis frequency k completes exactly k cycles in N samples. [Chapter 8, Notation and Format of the Real DFT through Synthesis, Eqs. 8-1–8-4]

A finite input to the DFT is mathematically treated as one period of an infinitely repeated discrete signal. This convention is often physically meaningless but becomes essential for understanding circular symmetry and circular convolution. [Chapter 8, The Family of Fourier Transform]

DFT analysis is correlation with each cosine and sine basis function; synthesis rescales those components and adds them. The imaginary/sine convention includes a sign choice so that forward and inverse transforms align with the broader complex-transform convention. [Chapter 8, Synthesis through Duality]

Rectangular and polar frequency-domain forms contain identical information: magnitude is √(Re²+Im²), phase is atan2(Im,Re), and reconstruction uses Re=Mag cos θ and Im=Mag sin θ. Practical phase work must handle radians, quadrants, near-zero magnitude, 2π wrapping, and π jumps caused by a nonnegative magnitude definition. [Chapter 8, Polar Notation and Polar Nuisances, Eqs. 8-5–8-7]

Segment-averaged spectral analysis windows many fixed-length blocks, computes magnitude spectra, and averages them; random spectral noise falls as the square root of the number of averages while frequency resolution remains set by segment length. A longer single DFT improves bin spacing but not the noise level. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-1]

A window trades spectral leakage against resolution. Rectangular has the narrowest main lobe and largest sidelobes, Blackman has a wider lobe and lower sidelobes, Hamming lies between them, and flat-top sacrifices substantial resolution to measure peak amplitude accurately between DFT bins. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Figs. 9-4–9-5]

Frequency resolution has two distinct limits: DFT bin spacing and observation duration. Zero padding samples the same continuous spectral curve more densely but cannot provide the information that a longer nonzero record supplies for separating close tones. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-3]

A system's frequency response is the Fourier transform of its impulse response. Therefore x*h=y in time corresponds to XH=Y in frequency; zero-padding a finite impulse response provides denser samples of its continuous DTFT without changing the system. [Chapter 9, Frequency Response of Systems, Figs. 9-6–9-7]

DFT-domain multiplication implements circular convolution because the DFT treats time as periodic. To recover an N+M−1-sample linear convolution, both inputs must be zero-padded to at least that length before transformation. [Chapter 9, Convolution via the Frequency Domain, Figs. 9-8–9-9]

The Fourier transform is linear for every member of the transform family: scaling a signal scales its transform, and adding signals adds their transforms. Addition must be performed on real and imaginary parts, not directly on polar magnitudes and phases. [Chapter 10, Linearity of the Fourier Transform, Figs. 10-1–10-2]

A shift of s samples in time leaves the magnitude spectrum unchanged and adds the linear phase term 2πsf; equivalently, time position is encoded in phase slope. A signal symmetric about sample zero has zero phase, while left-right symmetry elsewhere produces linear phase. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase, Fig. 10-3]

Changing the sign of phase—complex conjugation—flips a time signal left-for-right. Therefore convolution uses A(f)B(f), correlation uses A(f)B*(f), and X(f)X*(f) produces a zero-phase spectrum corresponding to a symmetric autocorrelation-like time signal. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase]

The DFT alone treats both domains as periodic: sample N−1 neighbors sample 0, and a one-period view is only safe when operations do not overflow a period. Excess extent wraps into adjacent periods as time-domain or frequency-domain aliasing. [Chapter 10, Periodic Nature of the DFT, Figs. 10-8–10-10]

Discrete sinusoids admit positive-, negative-, and infinitely many aliased-frequency descriptions that pass through the same samples. The ordinary 0-to-0.5 spectrum is one selected interval of a periodic frequency domain, not the only mathematical description. [Chapter 10, Periodic Nature of the DFT, Fig. 10-11]

Compression in one domain expands the other. For discrete signals this statement is conditioned on aliasing and on an assumed underlying continuous waveform; interpolation and decimation are resampling interpretations of the same relationship. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-12]

Frequency-domain zero padding interpolates a frequency-encoded time sequence without adding frequencies: Smith's 50-to-400-sample recipe pads to a 64-point DFT, extends its 33-bin real and imaginary spectra to 257 bins, and applies a 512-point inverse DFT. Discontinuities ring because the periodic bandlimited interpolant exhibits Gibbs behavior. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-13]

Multiplication in time corresponds to convolution in frequency. In amplitude modulation, multiplication by a carrier shifts the baseband spectrum to the carrier, producing carrier, upper sideband, and lower sideband; the lower sideband makes the otherwise abstract negative-frequency copy operationally visible. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation), Fig. 10-14]

The DTFT is the transform between an aperiodic discrete time signal and a periodic continuous spectrum. It appears as the zero-padded DFT limit as N approaches infinity and is principally an analytic tool because its sums and integrals are infinite. [Chapter 10, The Discrete Time Fourier Transform, Eqs. 10-1–10-2]

Parseval's relation expresses conservation of signal energy between the time and frequency domains; for Smith's real-DFT convention, DC and Nyquist require special √2 endpoint scaling and the spectrum-side energy sum carries a 2/N factor. [Chapter 10, Parseval's Relation, Eq. 10-3]

A time-domain impulse transforms to constant magnitude and linear phase; its sample position sets the number of sinusoidal cycles in the rectangular real/imaginary spectrum. By DFT duality, every time sample contributes one cosine to the real spectrum and one negative sine to the imaginary spectrum. [Chapter 11, Delta Function Pairs, Figs. 11-1–11-2]

A rectangular pulse and a sinc are a transform pair. The exact discrete spectrum includes aliasing through sin(πf) in the denominator; replacing that factor by πf gives the unaliased continuous approximation. The first spectral zero occurs where one complete sinusoidal cycle fits inside the pulse. [Chapter 11, The Sinc Function, Eqs. 11-1–11-2 and Figs. 11-3–11-4]

A rectangular frequency response corresponds to the sinc impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter. A triangle transforms to sinc squared because the triangle is the self-convolution of a rectangle; a Gaussian is its own transform shape with 2πσ_f=1/σ_t; and modulating a Gaussian by a sinusoid shifts its Gaussian spectrum. [Chapter 11, Other Transform Pairs, Eqs. 11-3–11-4 and Fig. 11-5]

At a discontinuity, a partial Fourier reconstruction rings and overshoots by roughly 9%. Adding harmonics narrows the ringing but does not reduce its peak; the continuous limit converges to the step midpoint at the discontinuity and to zero total error energy. [Chapter 11, Gibbs Effect, Fig. 11-6]

A waveform periodic at f contains only harmonics at integer multiples of f. Horizontal antisymmetry eliminates even harmonics, while nonlinear processing of sampled data can create above-Nyquist harmonics that alias back and masquerade as low-level noise. [Chapter 11, Harmonics, Figs. 11-7–11-8]

The chirp system has unit magnitude response and parabolic phase, yielding an impulse response whose instantaneous frequency sweeps with time. The phase-conjugate antichirp reverses it, enabling radar pulse compression: transmitter hardware handles a long energetic chirp while the receiver recovers a narrow timing pulse. [Chapter 11, Chirp Signals, Eq. 11-7 and Figs. 11-9–11-10]

A real N-point time signal can be transformed with a complex FFT by putting it in the real input array and zeroing the imaginary input. The useful real-DFT bins are 0 through N/2; the remaining complex-DFT bins are generated by even symmetry in the real part and odd symmetry in the imaginary part. [Chapter 12, Real DFT Using the Complex DFT, Fig. 12-1 and Table 12-1]

The radix-2 FFT recursively separates even and odd samples through log2 N stages, equivalent to bit-reversal reordering. It then synthesizes one-point spectra with butterfly operations that duplicate spectra, apply phase-shift sinusoids, and add paired results. [Chapter 12, How the FFT Works, Figs. 12-2–12-7]

The presented FFT is an in-place computation: the real and imaginary input arrays are overwritten by intermediate and output data. Variants such as decimation-in-time and decimation-in-frequency move bit reversal but produce the same DFT and comparable performance. [Chapter 12, FFT Programs, Tables 12-3–12-4]

A forward FFT can implement the inverse FFT by negating the imaginary spectrum, applying the forward transform, dividing both time-domain parts by N, and negating the imaginary output again. Round-trip reconstruction and expected even/odd symmetries are the chapter's two essential correctness tests. [Chapter 12, FFT Programs, Table 12-5]

Direct correlation computes the DFT in O(N²), while the FFT takes O(N log2 N). In the book's 100 MHz Pentium benchmark, a 1024-point transform drops from about 25 seconds to about 70 milliseconds—over 300× faster—and fewer operations also reduce roundoff error. [Chapter 12, Speed and Precision Comparisons, Eqs. 12-1–12-2 and Figs. 12-8–12-9]

Real-FFT variants exploit zero imaginary input and conjugate symmetry for about a 30% speed improvement; packing two real sequences into the real and imaginary input parts and separating their spectra with even/odd decomposition saves about 40% when two transforms are needed. [Chapter 12, Further Speed Increases, Figs. 12-10–12-11]

The continuous delta is defined operationally as an infinitesimally brief, unit-area impulse at zero. Real inputs act as impulses only relative to a slower system; their exact shape becomes irrelevant while output amplitude scales with input area. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function, Fig. 13-1]

Continuous convolution is the integral y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. Its input-side interpretation sums shifted, scaled impulse responses; its output-side interpretation integrates the input weighted by a flipped and shifted impulse response. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Eq. 13-1 and Figs. 13-2–13-3]

For an RC low-pass, h(t)=αe^(−αt) for t≥0 and zero before, with α=1/RC. Convolution with a one-second rectangular pulse must be evaluated in no-overlap, partial-overlap, and full-overlap regions, yielding an exponential charge followed by exponential discharge. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Figs. 13-4–13-6]

Continuous convolution problems can be simplified by differentiating piecewise-polynomial inputs into impulses, convolving by inspection, and integrating the result; constants of integration must restore lost DC terms. If only a waveform is required, discretizing and numerically convolving may be more useful than forcing a closed form. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Fig. 13-7]

For continuous aperiodic signals, Fourier synthesis integrates scaled sine and cosine waves over continuous frequency, while analysis correlates the signal with those sinusoids over all time. Transforming the RC impulse response gives its familiar low-pass magnitude and phase. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Transform, Eqs. 13-2–13-3 and Figs. 13-8–13-9]

The Fourier series represents a continuous periodic signal with a DC term plus sine and cosine harmonics of its fundamental. The coefficients are correlations over any one complete period; even signals need only cosine coefficients and odd signals only sine coefficients. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series, Eqs. 13-4–13-5]

Every linear filter is equivalently specified by impulse, step, or frequency response: running-summing the impulse response gives the step response, and transforming it gives the frequency response. Convolution implementations are FIR; recursive implementations are generally IIR even though both still possess an impulse response. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics, Fig. 14-1]

Decibels express ratios: 10log10(P2/P1) for power and 20log10(A2/A1) for amplitude. Thus −3 dB corresponds to amplitude 0.707 and half power, while each ±20 dB is a factor of ten in amplitude. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics, Eq. 14-1]

Filter design begins by locating the information: time-domain information is carried by when events occur and by waveform amplitude, whereas frequency-domain information is carried by relationships among many samples. These incompatible encodings make step response the primary criterion for the former and frequency response for the latter. [Chapter 14, How Information Is Represented in Signals]

Time-domain filter quality is judged by 10–90% risetime, overshoot, and linear-phase symmetry between rising and falling edges. Frequency-domain quality is judged by transition width/roll-off, passband ripple, and stopband attenuation. These objectives inherently trade against one another. [Chapter 14, Time Domain Parameters and Frequency Domain Parameters, Figs. 14-2–14-4]

Spectral inversion converts a symmetric low-pass FIR kernel h[n] to high-pass by forming δ[n]−h[n]; spectral reversal multiplies alternate kernel samples by −1, shifting the response by half the sampling rate. Adding low- and high-pass kernels forms band-reject, while convolving them forms band-pass. [Chapter 14, High-Pass, Band-Pass and Band-Reject Filters, Figs. 14-5–14-9]

Smith classifies filters by both purpose and implementation: moving-average FIR versus single-pole IIR for time-domain work, windowed-sinc FIR versus Chebyshev IIR for frequency separation, and direct custom FIR versus iterative recursive design for specialized responses. [Chapter 14, Filter Classification, Table 14-1]

An M-point moving average is convolution with a unit-area rectangular kernel; symmetric placement avoids relative delay but requires odd M. The direct implementation performs M additions per output, with output boundaries shortened by the kernel support. [Chapter 15, Implementation by Convolution, Eq. 15-1 and Table 15-1]

For white random noise, an M-point average reduces noise standard deviation by √M. Given a fixed edge width, equal weighting is optimal because no independent noisy sample deserves preference, making the moving average optimal for noise reduction at a specified step sharpness. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response, Fig. 15-1]

The moving-average response is sin(πfM)/(M sin πf): excellent for smoothing but poor for frequency separation because roll-off is slow and stopband sidelobes are large. [Chapter 15, Frequency Response, Eq. 15-2 and Fig. 15-2]

Repeated moving averages convolve rectangular kernels into a triangle and then a Gaussian-like shape; each pass multiplies the frequency response. Gaussian and Blackman kernels improve stopband behavior but retain roughly comparable noise-versus-edge performance and require slower direct convolution. [Chapter 15, Relatives of the Moving Average Filter, Figs. 15-3–15-4]

A moving average admits the O(1)-per-sample recursion y[i]=y[i−1]+x[i+p]−x[i−q]. Integer arithmetic avoids accumulated roundoff; a floating-point version should preserve the running sum in double precision to prevent a drifting offset. [Chapter 15, Recursive Implementation, Eq. 15-3 and Table 15-2]

A windowed-sinc low-pass begins with the ideal rectangular response and infinite sinc kernel, truncates and shifts the kernel, then multiplies it by a smooth window to suppress the endpoint discontinuity responsible for Gibbs ripple. [Chapter 16, Strategy of the Windowed-Sinc, Fig. 16-1]

The Hamming window rolls off about 20% faster, but Blackman provides materially better passband/stopband error: roughly 0.02% (−74 dB stopband) versus Hamming's 0.2% (−53 dB). Smith recommends Blackman when a slightly longer kernel is acceptable. [Chapter 16, Strategy of the Windowed-Sinc, Eqs. 16-1–16-2 and Fig. 16-2]

For the book's windowed-sinc design convention, kernel span M is approximately 4/BW, with BW measured across the 99%-to-1% transition and cutoff defined at half amplitude. M is even, the kernel has M+1 samples, and coefficients are normalized so their sum is one. [Chapter 16, Designing the Filter, Eqs. 16-3–16-4]

The symmetric windowed-sinc kernel provides linear phase but an oscillatory, overshooting step response. It is therefore a frequency-separation filter, not a good choice when waveform shape carries the information. [Chapter 16, Designing the Filter, Fig. 16-4]

The worked EEG design separates 7–12 Hz alpha rhythm from 17–20 Hz beta rhythm at 100 samples/s with a 101-point Hamming low-pass near 14 Hz; the audio signaling example uses an 801-point Blackman band-pass to isolate 1960–2040 Hz at a 10 kHz sample rate with 50 Hz transitions. [Chapter 16, Examples of Windowed-Sinc Filters, Figs. 16-5–16-6 and Tables 16-1–16-2]

Cascading identical windowed-sinc filters squares their magnitude response: two −74 dB Blackman stages yield roughly −148 dB stopband attenuation. Extremely long kernels can make transitions arbitrarily sharp, with execution time and numerical precision—not unexpected instability—as the main limits. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit, Fig. 16-7]

An arbitrary FIR response is designed by specifying magnitude and phase samples, applying an inverse FFT, circularly shifting the aliased impulse response, truncating it, and windowing it. Re-transforming a zero-padded kernel tests the actual continuous response; increasing kernel length improves the match between specified samples. [Chapter 17, Arbitrary Frequency Response, Tables 17-1 and Figs. 17-1–17-2]

Known-system deconvolution divides the desired output spectrum by the unwanted system response using complex division, then designs a practical FIR kernel from that quotient. It becomes unstable where the original system strongly attenuates or nulls frequencies, because inverse gain amplifies modeling error and noise. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Figs. 17-4–17-5]

Blind deconvolution has no general solution because the parasitic response is unknown. The Caruso restoration example estimates recording-horn coloration by comparing averaged old-recording and modern-reference spectra, with homomorphic processing used in the cited historical work for a better estimate. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Fig. 17-6]

Different filters are optimal under different objective functions: moving average gives the fastest step for a noise reduction, matched filtering maximizes peak detectability in white noise, and Wiener filtering uses H(f)=S²/(S²+N²) to maximize overall output signal-to-noise power. [Chapter 17, Optimal Filters, Eq. 17-1 and Figs. 17-7–17-9]

Overlap-add partitions a long input into zero-padded blocks, convolves each independently, and sums their overlapping output tails. Because an N-sample block convolved with an M-sample kernel produces N+M−1 samples, adequate padding is what makes the segmented result exactly equal to full direct convolution. [Chapter 18, The Overlap-Add Method, Fig. 18-1]

FFT convolution replaces each block's direct convolution with FFT → complex spectral multiplication → inverse FFT. Transform length must be at least the output-block length to prevent circular wraparound; a 128-point block and 129-point kernel therefore use 256-point FFTs. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Fig. 18-2]

The full program example filters 10,000,000 samples with a 400-point kernel using 16,000 blocks of 625 input samples and 1024-point transforms, retaining 399 samples of overlap between blocks and producing 10,000,399 output samples. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Table 18-1]

The implementation crossover is hardware-dependent but lies around 40–80 kernel samples; Smith's rule of thumb is direct convolution below roughly 60 and FFT convolution above it. FFT convolution's operation count grows slowly enough that a 16,000-point kernel costs only about twice a 64-point kernel, and fewer operations also reduce roundoff. [Chapter 18, Speed Improvements, Fig. 18-3]

A recursive filter computes each output sample from present and past input samples plus previously computed output samples; the feedforward a coefficients and feedback b coefficients together define the recursion. Reusing output samples produces a long, usually exponentially decaying impulse response with only a few arithmetic operations. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method, Eq. 19-1 and Table 19-1]

Recursive filters are called IIR because their ideal impulse responses continue indefinitely, whereas convolution filters are FIR. Smith's practical rule is that the IIR response can usually be truncated after roughly 15-20 time constants, once it falls below single-precision round-off noise. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method; Phase Response, pp. 320, 325, and 332]

For a one-pole low-pass filter, a0 = 1-x and b1 = x; for the corresponding high-pass filter, a0 = (1+x)/2, a1 = -(1+x)/2, and b1 = x. The parameter 0<x<1 is the sample-to-sample decay. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eqs. 19-2 and 19-3]

The one-pole decay parameter can be selected from a time constant d in samples by x = exp(-1/d), or from normalized -3 dB cutoff frequency fc by x = exp(-2πfc). This makes the digital filter directly analogous to an RC network. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eqs. 19-4 and 19-5]

Cascading four one-pole low-pass stages improves stopband attenuation and retains fast execution, but the roll-off is still poor compared with a true frequency-selective filter. Smith supplies the combined coefficients a0=(1-x)^4 and b1=4x, b2=-6x^2, b3=4x^3, b4=-x^4. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Fig. 19-5 and Eq. 19-6]

Second-order band-pass and band-reject filters are parameterized by normalized center frequency f and bandwidth BW through R=1-3BW and a gain term K. They are effective for tones such as 60 Hz interference, but single precision limits the narrowest useful bandwidth to about 0.0003 of the sampling frequency. [Chapter 19, Narrow-band Filters, Eqs. 19-7 and 19-8 and Fig. 19-6]

Zero-phase impulse responses are symmetric about sample zero; linear-phase responses are shifted symmetric responses; asymmetric impulse responses have nonlinear phase and distort the two edges of a pulse differently. FIR symmetry makes exact linear phase easy, while causal IIR responses are inherently asymmetric. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Fig. 19-7]

Any recursive filter can be made zero phase off-line by filtering forward and then backward. The phase cancels, the magnitude response is squared, and execution time approximately doubles; streamed blocks require overlap-add and padding on both sides. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Eq. 19-9 and Fig. 19-8]

Integer IIR implementations face both coefficient representation and accumulated round-off/instability problems. Smith suggests rational coefficients or lookup tables, but recommends checking whether the recursive moving average can meet the requirement first because it is naturally integer-friendly. [Chapter 19, Using Integers]

A type-I Chebyshev response buys a faster transition by allowing passband ripple; setting ripple to zero gives the maximally flat Butterworth response. Smith recommends 0.5% ripple as a practical compromise and notes that elliptic filters achieve still faster roll-off by allowing ripple in both bands. [Chapter 20, The Chebyshev and Butterworth Responses, Fig. 20-1]

Chebyshev design in this chapter is determined by four choices: low-pass or high-pass, normalized cutoff, percent passband ripple, and an even number of poles. Cutoff is measured at amplitude 0.707 (-3 dB); more poles sharpen the transition, and filters near normalized 0 or 0.5 roll off faster for a given pole count. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter, Fig. 20-2]

The cookbook design constructs complex-conjugate pole pairs, warps the Butterworth circle into a Chebyshev ellipse when ripple is nonzero, maps from the s-domain to the z-domain, transforms low-pass to low- or high-pass, combines stages, and normalizes gain. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter, Tables 20-4 and 20-5]

Frequency-domain optimization costs time-domain behavior: Chebyshev step-response overshoot is about 5%-30%, depending mainly on pole count and somewhat on cutoff frequency. [Chapter 20, Step Response Overshoot, Fig. 20-3]

Round-off noise limits the safe pole count, especially near normalized cutoff 0 or 0.5. Smith's single-precision guide allows approximately 4 poles at 0.02/0.48, 6 at 0.05/0.45, 10 at 0.10/0.40, and 20 at 0.25. [Chapter 20, Stability, Table 20-3]

Higher-order recursive filters are made more stable by double precision or, preferably, by retaining the cascade of second-order sections instead of combining all pole pairs into one high-order recursion. [Chapter 20, Stability, Tables 20-4 through 20-6]

For comparable low-pass jobs, digital filters can be much flatter, steeper, and more linear-phase than analog filters; analog filters retain advantages in speed, very wide dynamic range, simplicity, and operation before sampling or after reconstruction. [Chapter 21, Match #1: Analog vs. Digital Filters, Fig. 21-1]

At moderate specifications a windowed-sinc FIR and Chebyshev IIR can both work. At extreme specifications the FIR can be extended to nearly arbitrary attenuation while the IIR reaches numerical/performance limits; the IIR is commonly about an order of magnitude faster at comparable performance. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev, Figs. 21-2 through 21-5]

For time-domain smoothing, a moving average gives the fastest straight-line step transition, while a bidirectional one-pole filter gives a smoother rounded transition. The choice often turns on implementation: floating-point one-off work favors the easy recursive filter, while highly optimized integer products favor the moving average. [Chapter 21, Match #3: Moving Average vs. Single Pole, Figs. 21-6 and 21-7]

The cochlea's basilar membrane implements place coding: stiffness varies along its length so different locations respond to different frequencies. Neural firing also implements volley coding below roughly 4 kHz, with individual neurons limited to about 500 action potentials per second. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Fig. 22-1]

Human hearing spans roughly 20 Hz-20 kHz and about 120 dB in intensity, yet resolves only about 120 loudness steps. Sensitivity peaks around 1-4 kHz; binaural direction uses head shadow above about 1 kHz and interaural delay below it. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Table 22-1]

Timbre is governed by harmonic amplitudes, not a unique waveform. Signals with identical component magnitudes but different relative phases normally sound the same because environmental propagation randomizes phase; one timbre can therefore correspond to infinitely many waveforms. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Figs. 22-2 and 22-3]

Audio information is approximately logarithmic in frequency. Each octave carries comparable perceptual information, explaining why telephone speech can retain intelligibility over 200 Hz-3.2 kHz even though it discards most of the linear 20 kHz bandwidth. [Chapter 22, Timbre; Sound Quality vs. Data Rate, Fig. 22-4]

Smith's reference data rates are 706 kbit/s for mono 44.1 kHz, 16-bit high-fidelity audio; 96 kbit/s for 8 kHz, 12-bit telephone speech; 64 kbit/s after 8-bit companding; and about 4 kbit/s for LPC-compressed speech. [Chapter 22, Sound Quality vs. Data Rate, Table 22-2]

CD playback expands 8 data bits to 14 by EFM to control pit run lengths, uses Reed-Solomon redundancy for correction/concealment, recovers 16-bit 44.1 kHz samples, and commonly interpolates by four before a simpler analog reconstruction filter. [Chapter 22, High Fidelity Audio, Figs. 22-5 and 22-6]

Companding matches quantization steps to logarithmic hearing: telephone-quality speech can use 8 unequal bits instead of 12 uniform bits. North American μ255 law and European A-law are nearly identical except near zero; their mappings are given explicitly. [Chapter 22, Companding, Eqs. 22-1 and 22-2 and Fig. 22-7]

Voiced speech consists of quasi-periodic vocal-cord excitation shaped by resonances of the vocal tract; fricatives are noise-like. Spectrograms expose changing formants, while recognition remains harder than matching isolated acoustic patterns because human listeners exploit context and expectations. [Chapter 22, Speech Synthesis and Recognition, Figs. 22-8 and 22-9]

Wideband speech noise can be reduced by short-time, time-varying spectral weighting: large spectral components are treated as signal, small ones as noise, and overlapping windowed frames are recombined smoothly. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Fig. 22-10]

Homomorphic processing linearizes multiplicative mixtures with a logarithm and convolutional mixtures with Fourier transform followed by logarithm. Linear filtering can then separate components before the transforms are inverted, but nonlinearities create aliasing and overlapping harmonics that may defeat separation. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Figs. 22-11 and 22-12]

A digital image is a two-dimensional array of pixels whose values encode a physical parameter. Smith treats the spatial domain as primary: image information is carried mainly by edges and regions, not sinusoids. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]

Sample spacing and sampling aperture are independent: the grid says where measurements are taken, while the aperture says what surrounding region contributes to each pixel. Final resolution is limited by the worse of the two. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]

Eight-bit grayscale is usually adequate for display because 1/256 brightness steps are below visual discrimination and spatial dithering averages neighboring values, though scientific acquisition may need more bits to preserve nonvisual information. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure]

Cameras and eyes share a lens, adjustable aperture, and sensor, but the eye achieves most of its huge dynamic range by adapting receptor sensitivity rather than by pupil area alone. Reflection images can be modeled as reflectance multiplied by illumination, motivating later illumination flattening. [Chapter 23, Cameras and Eyes, Figs. 23-2 through 23-6]

Brightness adds an offset to every pixel; contrast changes the slope around a chosen midpoint. Both are point operations implementable by a 256-entry lookup table, with clipping when transformed values exceed the display range. [Chapter 23, Brightness and Contrast Adjustments, Figs. 23-10 through 23-12]

A grayscale transform allocates output contrast according to the slope of its lookup curve. A desired contrast weighting is integrated and normalized to construct the transform; histogram equalization automates this by integrating the image histogram and maximizes entropy, but can neglect semantically important rare pixels. [Chapter 23, Grayscale Transforms, Figs. 23-13 and 23-14]

Warping computes, for each destination pixel, a comes-from address in the source. Nearest-neighbor sampling is simple but jagged; bilinear interpolation combines the four surrounding source pixels and gives the same result regardless of whether horizontal or vertical interpolation is performed first. [Chapter 23, Warping, Figs. 23-15 and 23-16]

Two-dimensional convolution carries over the impulse-response view: the image impulse response is the point spread function (PSF), and every input pixel contributes a scaled, shifted PSF to the output. In the output-side view, the PSF is flipped horizontally and vertically. [Chapter 24, Convolution; A Closer Look at Image Convolution, Eq. 24-3 and Figs. 24-14 and 24-15]

Common smoothing PSFs are pillbox, Gaussian, and square kernels; edge enhancement follows spectral inversion by negating a smoothing kernel and adding a centered impulse. Retinal lateral inhibition is a biological edge enhancer and creates Mach bands. [Chapter 24, Convolution, Figs. 24-1 through 24-3]

A 3x3 PSF is enough for many edge operations, including gradient-like edge detection and sharpening, because it reaches immediate neighbors while requiring only nine multiply-accumulates per output pixel. [Chapter 24, 3x3 Edge Modification, Fig. 24-4]

A PSF is separable when h[r,c]=vert[r]horz[c]. Convolving rows and then columns reduces work for an N by N image and M by M kernel from proportional to N²M² to N²M; the Gaussian is the only circularly symmetric separable PSF. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability, Eq. 24-1 and Figs. 24-5 through 24-7]

Rectangular and double-sided-exponential separable kernels can be implemented recursively, making cost proportional to N² and independent of PSF width; repeated applications approach a Gaussian by the central limit theorem. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability]

Uneven illumination can be estimated with a very broad smoothing PSF. Subtracting that estimate approximates reflectance linearly, while dividing the viewed image by the illumination estimate better matches the multiplicative formation model but is nonlinear. [Chapter 24, Example of a Large PSF: Illumination Flattening, Fig. 24-8]

A two-dimensional DFT is computed by applying one-dimensional FFTs to every row and then every column (or vice versa). Typical image spectra look unintuitive because the source information is spatial; Fourier analysis is most useful for convolution/deconvolution and projection relationships. [Chapter 24, Fourier Image Analysis, Figs. 24-9 and 24-10 and Eq. 24-2]

FFT correlation zero-pads image and target to contain the full linear convolution, transforms both, multiplies complex spectra, and inverse-transforms. Edge-filtering the target sharpens the correlation peak, but exact target size and orientation remain critical. [Chapter 24, FFT Convolution, Figs. 24-11 through 24-13]

Conventional image convolution costs O(N²M²); FFT convolution costs approximately O(N² log N). In Smith's example, FFT becomes worthwhile around a 10x10 kernel versus floating-point direct convolution, or around 30x30 versus integer direct convolution. [Chapter 24, A Closer Look at Image Convolution, Fig. 24-16]

Spatial resolution can be described by PSF full-width at half maximum, MTF limiting frequency, line-spread width, or 10%-90% edge-response distance. Smith favors edge response because it matches how image information is encoded, is easy to acquire, and converts to MTF through first difference plus a one-dimensional FFT. [Chapter 25, Spatial Resolution, Figs. 25-1 through 25-5]

Resolution is aperture-limited when more than about three samples span a 10%-90% edge, spacing-limited when fewer than one sample spans it, and jointly limited between one and three samples. A sufficiently broad aperture acts as an antialias filter. [Chapter 25, Sample Spacing and Sampling Aperture, Fig. 25-6]

Detectability depends on object contrast divided by noise standard deviation and begins to fail around SNR=1. Smoothing with a kernel matched to object size improves SNR by the square root of the number of averaged pixels, so detectability scales with the square root of object area. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Figs. 25-7 and 25-8]

Counting (Poisson) noise has standard deviation equal to the square root of the mean count, hence SNR equal to the square root of the count. Improving SNR by a factor of two therefore requires four times as many photons, x-rays, or electrons. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Eq. 25-1 and Fig. 25-9]

Binary morphology uses erosion to shrink/break objects, dilation to expand/merge them, opening (erosion then dilation) to remove small object islands and thin protrusions, and closing (dilation then erosion) to fill small holes and gaps. [Chapter 25, Morphological Image Processing, Fig. 25-10]

Skeletonization iteratively removes boundary pixels while preserving endpoints and connectivity; Smith's implementation marks removable pixels first and deletes them only after scanning the whole image to avoid directional bias. [Chapter 25, Morphological Image Processing, Figs. 25-11 and 25-12 and Tables 25-1 and 25-2]

Each CT view sample is a line integral through the slice. Filtered backprojection filters every view before smearing it back along its acquisition rays, exactly reconstructing the ideal image in the limit of infinitely many samples and views. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-14 through 25-17]

The Fourier slice theorem states that the one-dimensional spectrum of a projection is a radial slice through the two-dimensional image spectrum at the same angle. Backprojection's radial sampling density varies as 1/f, so the correction filter has magnitude proportional to f, with the kernel specified by Eq. 25-2. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-18 and 25-19 and Eq. 25-2]

Target and nontarget distributions must be combined with prevalence/base rates when turning a test value into probability. Ignoring a rare target's prior probability can change a seemingly 25% posterior to 0.025% in Smith's cancer-test example. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Fig. 26-1]

Threshold choice trades false positives against false negatives. An ROC curve plots target-positive rate against nontarget-positive rate across thresholds; better systems bend toward the upper-left, while random guessing follows the diagonal. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Figs. 26-2 through 26-4]

Smith's standard neural network is fully connected input-hidden-output: passive input nodes fan out, active nodes form weighted sums, and a sigmoid maps each sum to 0-1. A bias input of one shifts sigmoid thresholds. [Chapter 26, Neural Network Architecture, Figs. 26-5 through 26-7, Eqs. 26-1 and 26-2]

The hidden layer can be interpreted as a bank of correlators followed by smooth probability-like thresholds, and the output layer as a correlation of correlations—a detector of patterns of patterns. The nonlinearity is essential; without it, adjacent linear layers collapse into one. [Chapter 26, Neural Network Architecture; Why Does It Work?]

Training is optimization over examples, not derivation of human-readable rules. Smith's vowel detector uses 100 pixels plus a bias, 10 hidden nodes, one output, and 1,020 learned weights, with separate training and test images. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Fig. 26-8 and Tables 26-2 and 26-3]

Steepest descent updates each weight in proportion to output sensitivity, current example error, and step size μ. Backpropagated slopes use the sigmoid derivative s'(x)=s(x)(1-s(x)); too large μ oscillates/diverges and too small μ converges slowly. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Eqs. 26-3 through 26-5 and Fig. 26-9]

Network quality must be measured on held-out examples and across thresholds, not only by training error. In Smith's best trial, a point on the ROC curve detects 96% of vowels with 4% false positives; random initialization causes materially different solutions. [Chapter 26, Evaluating the Results, Figs. 26-10 through 26-12]

Custom IIR magnitude responses can be designed by finite-difference steepest descent on recursion coefficients: impulse-response FFT gives the current magnitude, RMS spectral error defines the objective, and μ is reduced when a step worsens error. Initial coefficients must describe a stable system. [Chapter 26, Recursive Filter Design, Tables 26-4 and 26-5 and Fig. 26-13]

Compression is classified both by fidelity (lossless versus lossy) and by whether input/output group sizes are fixed or variable. Lossless methods must reconstruct every bit; lossy methods trade controlled signal degradation for much higher compression. [Chapter 27, Data Compression Strategies, Table 27-1]

Run-length encoding replaces a run by a value/flag and count; it compresses only when runs are long enough and can enlarge data dominated by isolated occurrences. PackBits generalizes the idea by using a signed count convention. [Chapter 27, Run-Length Encoding, Fig. 27-1]

Huffman coding assigns shorter prefix-free codes to more probable symbols, with ideal code length proportional to the negative logarithm of symbol probability. Proper prefix selection lets a variable-length bitstream be decoded without explicit delimiters. [Chapter 27, Huffman Encoding, Fig. 27-3]

Delta encoding stores the first sample and then successive differences. For slowly varying signals it concentrates values near zero, making subsequent Huffman or run-length coding more effective; linear predictive coding generalizes the predictor from the previous sample to several past samples. [Chapter 27, Delta Encoding, Figs. 27-4–27-5]

LZW is a lossless dictionary method that starts with single-byte codes, emits fixed-width codes for the longest known strings, and builds matching code tables during compression and decompression, so the dictionary need not be transmitted separately. [Chapter 27, LZW Compression, Figs. 27-6–27-8 and Table 27-3]

JPEG transform compression partitions an image into 8×8 blocks, applies a 2-D DCT, quantizes coefficients more aggressively at high spatial frequencies, serializes coefficients in zigzag order, run-length encodes zero runs, and finishes with Huffman or arithmetic coding. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Figs. 27-9–27-14]

The DCT is advantageous for block image compression because its lowest nonconstant basis functions contain half cycles and therefore model gradual brightness ramps more economically than the Fourier transform's full-cycle lowest frequencies. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Fig. 27-10 and printed p. 501]

MPEG combines intraframe JPEG-like compression with interframe prediction: I-pictures are independently coded, P-pictures refer to earlier frames, and B-pictures can refer to both earlier and later frames. [Chapter 27, MPEG, printed p. 502]

Real-time DSP differs from offline computation because it must sustain the input sample rate indefinitely; extra throughput costs power, money, and design effort, so the relevant requirement is a bounded cycles-per-sample budget. [Chapter 28, How DSPs Are Different from Other Microprocessors]

A real-time FIR filter maintains recent samples and coefficients in circular buffers. Each output requires interrupt handling, two circular-buffer fetch/update streams, multiply-accumulate work, and loop control; DSP hardware is arranged to execute many of these operations in parallel. [Chapter 28, Circular Buffering, Fig. 28-3 and Table 28-1]

Harvard architecture separates instruction and data memories so an instruction and data can be fetched simultaneously; Super Harvard architecture adds an instruction cache and an I/O controller, freeing buses and supporting concurrent computation and data transfer. [Chapter 28, Architecture of the Digital Signal Processor, Figs. 28-4–28-5]

DSP address generators provide zero-overhead circular and bit-reversed addressing, while parallel multiplier, ALU, barrel shifter, register files, and shadow registers support one-cycle multiply-accumulate loops and low-latency interrupts. [Chapter 28, Architecture of the Digital Signal Processor]

A 16-bit fixed-point representation offers uniformly spaced values and low device cost; 32-bit IEEE floating point offers vastly greater dynamic range, relative precision, and easier development because scaling, overflow, and underflow require less manual management. [Chapter 28, Fixed versus Floating Point, Fig. 28-6]

Repeated quantization can dominate fixed-point DSP. The text estimates storage SNR near 30 million-to-one for 32-bit floating point versus about ten-thousand-to-one for 16-bit fixed point, and explains why extended accumulators retain intermediate precision. [Chapter 28, Fixed versus Floating Point]

C improves portability and development speed while assembly exposes maximum hardware parallelism. Efficient DSP C still requires architecture-aware declarations and memory placement; performance must be checked on the actual compiler and target. [Chapter 28, C versus Assembly, Tables 28-2–28-4]

Algorithm throughput is clock rate divided by cycles per sample, not a generic MIPS/MFLOPS headline. On the chapter's 40 MHz SHARC example, conventional FIR throughput spans roughly 100 thousand to 1.6 million samples/s, IIR about 1.8–3.1 million, and FFT routines about 1.8–3.3 million. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?, Fig. 28-11]

For the worked 512-sample overlap-add configuration, FFT convolution costs about 60 cycles/sample; this makes direct convolution faster below roughly 60 taps and FFT convolution faster above it, with FFT cost then growing only logarithmically with kernel length. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

The ADSP-2106x case study emphasizes on-chip memory and I/O bandwidth as first-class design constraints: a 544-kbit SRAM holds about 6–8 seconds of 8-kHz, 8-bit speech, while 4 Mbits can hold a 512×512 8-bit image. [Chapter 29, The ADSP-2106x Family, Table 29-1]

The EZ-KIT workflow treats samples one at a time: a codec interrupt acquires fixed-point input, converts it to floating point, updates a circular delay line, performs a 301-tap parallel multiply-accumulate loop, converts back to fixed point, and returns the output to the codec. [Chapter 29, Design Example: An FIR Audio Filter, Table 29-2]

Symmetric FIR kernels produce exact linear phase: the 301-point example has its center at sample 150, hence a fixed delay of 150 samples, or 18.75 ms at 8 kHz. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System, Figs. 29-2–29-3]

The measured EZ-KIT response follows the designed custom FIR response within measurement error. The text contrasts ordinary bench-instrument accuracy of roughly 0.1–1% with the codec's roughly 0.001% roundoff scale, motivating higher-resolution acquisition for validating a digital implementation. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System, Fig. 29-4]

Floating-point execution can push implementation error below algorithm-design error; in the 150-tap Blackman-window example, floating-point roundoff is below the window's approximately 0.02% overshoot, whereas fixed-point coefficient quantization becomes the dominant imperfection. [Chapter 29, Another Look at Fixed versus Floating Point, Fig. 29-5]

FIR filters are comparatively insensitive to coefficient roundoff, while IIR feedback can amplify quantization enough to degrade cutoff, attenuation, overshoot, or even stability; this is a central reason to prefer floating point for sensitive recursive designs. [Chapter 29, Another Look at Fixed versus Floating Point, Figs. 29-5–29-6]

A complex number contains two real components and may be represented as a+jb or as magnitude/phase Me^{jθ}; rectangular form is convenient for addition, while polar/exponential form makes multiplication and division become magnitude products/ratios and angle sums/differences. [Chapter 30, The Complex Number System and Polar Notation, Eqs. 30-8–30-14]
Euler's relation e^{jx}=cos(x)+j sin(x) connects rectangular and polar forms and makes complex exponentials the compact language of sinusoidal DSP. [Chapter 30, Polar Notation, Eqs. 30-11–30-12]

Complex substitution is valid only after a physical problem has been shown to preserve the same algebraic structure; placing two arbitrary real quantities into real and imaginary parts does not license arbitrary complex multiplication. [Chapter 30, Using Complex Numbers by Substitution]

A sinusoid A cos(ωt)+B sin(ωt) maps to the complex value A−jB, or equivalently M e^{jφ}; multiplying by a system's complex response applies amplitude scaling and phase shift while automatically tracking sine/cosine cross-terms. [Chapter 30, Complex Representation of Sinusoids and Systems, Fig. 30-4]

For sinusoidal steady state, impedance turns differential component laws into algebra: resistor, capacitor, and inductor impedances are R, 1/(jωC), and jωL, and the phasor relation V=IZ acts as Ohm's law for magnitude and phase. [Chapter 30, Electrical Circuit Analysis, Fig. 30-5]

The RLC notch example obtains a complete frequency response by substituting impedances into an ordinary voltage-divider relation, illustrating why phasor algebra is simpler than solving the coupled differential equations directly. [Chapter 30, Electrical Circuit Analysis, Figs. 30-6–30-7]

Euler's identities express each real sine or cosine as the sum of equal-status positive- and negative-frequency complex exponentials; one-half of each conjugate frequency component is required to synthesize a unit real sinusoid. [Chapter 31, Mathematical Equivalence, Eqs. 31-3–31-4]

The complex DFT maps an N-point complex time sequence to an N-point complex periodic spectrum. Indices 0…N/2 represent nonnegative frequencies and N/2…N−1 represent wrapped negative frequencies. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT, Eqs. 31-5–31-8]

A unit real cosine produces two complex spectral components of amplitude one-half. DC and Nyquist are self-paired boundary samples, explaining why the real DFT needs special scaling there while the complex DFT does not. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT]

A real time-domain signal has conjugate-symmetric spectrum: its real spectral part is even and its imaginary part is odd. Conversely, an imaginary time-domain part produces odd-real/even-imaginary spectral symmetry, enabling two real FFTs to be packed into one complex FFT. [Chapter 31, The Complex DFT, Fig. 31-1]

The Fourier family is organized by discrete/continuous and periodic/aperiodic dualities: DFT, DTFT, Fourier series, and Fourier transform. Discreteness in one domain implies periodicity in the other, while continuity implies aperiodicity. [Chapter 31, The Family of Fourier Transforms, Table 31-1]

Each Fourier transform has analysis by correlation and synthesis by weighted sinusoids. Scaling may be placed on either direction; the chapter uses 1/N, 1/T, or 1/(2π) equivalents for complex forms and twice those values for positive-frequency-only real forms. [Chapter 31, The Family of Fourier Transforms, Table 31-1]

The Laplace transform generalizes the complex Fourier transform by correlating a continuous signal with exponentially weighted sinusoids. The imaginary axis σ=0 is exactly the Fourier transform, while other vertical lines use exponential growth or decay. [Chapter 32, The Nature of the s-Domain, Eq. 32-1 and Fig. 32-1]

For differential-equation systems, impulse responses are combinations of exponentials and sinusoids; the Laplace transform represents such a system compactly by poles and zeros rather than by every point of a waveform. [Chapter 32, opening and Strategy of the Laplace Transform]

A zero is a probing exponential-sinusoid that exactly cancels against the impulse response; a pole lies on the boundary where the transform ceases to converge. A stable causal continuous-time system has no poles in the right half of the s-plane. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform, Figs. 32-4–32-5]

Circuit analysis maps R, L, and C to R, sL, and 1/(sC), derives the transfer function H(s), evaluates H(jω) for frequency response, and uses partial fractions/inverse transforms for the impulse response. The phasor method is the σ=0 subset. [Chapter 32, Analysis of Electric Circuits, Figs. 32-6–32-8]

Pole-zero distance controls the s-plane response: the magnitude at a point is proportional to the product of distances to zeros divided by the product of distances to poles; phase is the corresponding sum of zero angles minus pole angles. [Chapter 32, The Importance of Poles and Zeros, Fig. 32-7]

A Sallen-Key biquad supplies two poles on a circle of radius 1/RC; amplifier gain moves them from the real axis toward the imaginary axis, sharpening and peaking the response until gain 3 places them on the axis and produces oscillation. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Eq. 32-4 and Fig. 32-9]

Classic analog low-pass designs have geometric pole-zero signatures: Butterworth poles are equally spaced on a left-half-plane circle, Chebyshev poles lie on a flattened ellipse to trade passband ripple for transition sharpness, and elliptic filters add imaginary-axis zeros to permit ripple in both bands for the sharpest transition. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Figs. 32-10–32-11]

The z-transform X(z)=Σx[n]z^{-n} is the discrete counterpart of the Laplace transform. Writing z=re^{jω} makes radius encode exponential growth/decay and angle encode frequency; vertical s-plane lines map to concentric z-plane circles. [Chapter 33, The Nature of the z-Domain, Eq. 33-1 and Figs. 33-1–33-2]

The unit circle r=1 in the z-plane is the discrete-time frequency-response contour. Stable recursive filters have poles inside it; moving conjugate poles toward unit-circle zeros narrows and sharpens a notch while preserving real coefficients. [Chapter 33, The Nature of the z-Domain and Analysis of Recursive Systems, Fig. 33-3]

A recursive difference equation maps directly to a rational transfer function whose numerator roots are zeros and denominator roots are poles. For a biquad, pole and zero radii/angles yield coefficients by simple cosine relations. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems, Eqs. 33-3–33-5]

To assess an implemented recursive filter, driving the actual coefficient realization with an impulse and FFTing the resulting response reveals roundoff-induced instability that merely evaluating ideal H(z) on the unit circle can miss. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems]

Cascade stages multiply transfer functions and parallel stages add them; polynomial coefficient multiplication is convolution, which turns stage composition into a compact coefficient-array algorithm. [Chapter 33, Cascade and Parallel Stages, Fig. 33-4 and Table 33-1]

Recursive spectral inversion subtracts a filter output from the original signal and changes numerator coefficients while retaining denominator coefficients, but unlike linear-phase FIR inversion it often performs poorly because phase prevents clean cancellation. [Chapter 33, Spectral Inversion, Eqs. 33-6–33-7 and Figs. 33-5–33-6]

Benford's law predicts P(first digit=d)=log10(d+1)−log10(d); thus 1 leads about 30.1% of values and 2 about 17.6%. Compliant datasets are scale invariant under multiplication by a constant. [Chapter 34, Frank Benford's Discovery, Figs. 34-1–34-2]

Homomorphic processing converts a difficult nonlinear-looking problem into a familiar linear system; for multiplication, taking a logarithm converts products into sums, and for Benford analysis the independent variable is moved to a logarithmic number line. [Chapter 34, Homomorphic Processing]

The Ones Scaling Test repeatedly rescales a dataset and records the fraction with leading digit 1. A compliant dataset remains near 0.301 for every scale; using factors of 1.01 makes the result periodic every roughly 232 steps because 1.01^{232}≈10. [Chapter 34, The Ones Scaling Test, Fig. 34-3 and Table 34-1]

On the base-10 log axis, leading-digit extraction is represented by a period-one sampling function. Shift–multiply–integrate makes the Ones Scaling Test the convolution ost(g)=sf(g)*pdf(−g). [Chapter 34, Writing Benford's Law as a Convolution, Eqs. 34-1–34-3 and Fig. 34-4]

Fourier transformation turns that convolution into OST(f)=SF(f)PDF*(f). Because sf(g) is period one, SF(f) is nonzero only at integer frequencies, reducing compliance to a sparse frequency-domain condition. [Chapter 34, Solving in the Frequency Domain, Eq. 34-4 and Fig. 34-5]

Benford's Law Compliance Theorem: a random process in base B follows Benford's law if and only if the Fourier transform of its log-domain PDF is zero at every nonzero integer frequency. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #2, printed p. 715]

The logarithmic leading-digit pattern comes from the periodic sampling function, not a hidden pattern in the original numbers: its DC value fixes log10(2)=0.301 for digit 1 and analogous log intervals for the other digits. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #1]

For ordinary smooth distributions, broad width on the log axis makes the frequency-domain PDF narrow enough to vanish near f=1, so broad distributions follow Benford better than narrow ones; oscillatory transforms provide an exceptional exact-compliance route. [Chapter 34, Solving Mystery #2 and More on Following Benford's Law, Figs. 34-6–34-7]

For the log-normal example, doubling log-domain 2σ width from 0.5 to 1.0 changes the Ones Scaling Test from a 16–45% swing to less than 1% fluctuation. Products of independent positive random variables naturally approach broad log-normal distributions via the central-limit effect in log space. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, Fig. 34-8]
pedagogy: An intuition-first, tool-building DSP course for scientists and engineers, organized as a long conceptual ramp from real signals to increasingly formal transform methods. Smith nearly always introduces an idea through a physical story, diagram, or failure mode, then supplies a compact equation, numerical design rule, BASIC-like program, and side-by-side plot. The progression is unusually deliberate: applications motivate statistics, conversion, and computer-number behavior; linearity licenses impulse and sinusoidal decomposition; convolution and the real DFT reconnect in frequency-domain filtering; transform properties and FFTs make practical FIR design possible; recursive filters, audio, imaging, compression, and simple neural networks show the machinery at work; hardware chapters trace cycles, buffers, and measurements; only then do complex numbers, the complex Fourier family, Laplace transform, and z-transform formalize the theory. Proofs are uncommon and constructive derivations dominate, ending in coefficients, code, or an experiment rather than abstraction for its own sake. Dense canonical diagrams, memorable analogies, complete worked traces, parameter sweeps, debugging tables, listening/visual comparisons, and measured data act as exercises-by-inspection; the book has no conventional end-of-chapter problem sets. Prerequisites begin with algebra, trigonometry, and general science literacy, then accumulate probability, calculus, convolution, Fourier analysis, programming, linear algebra, differential/difference equations, and complex variables as the sequence advances. The source is exceptionally useful for teaching judgment—time versus frequency information, precision versus accuracy, direct versus FFT convolution, FIR versus IIR, fixed versus floating point, and mathematical elegance versus implementation risk. A current adaptation should preserve those experiments and reasoning patterns while replacing historically dated BASIC syntax, processor prices and market forecasts, television/audio rates, software interfaces, patent notes, and product-selection advice with modern notebooks, hardware, and standards.
