gems: The T-carrier example turns multiplexing into arithmetic: each telephone voice is 8,000 samples/s × 8 bits = 64 kb/s; 24 voices fit into 1.544 Mb/s and travel about 6,000 feet on ordinary 22-gauge copper. [Chapter 1, Telecommunications]
Artificial reverberation is explained perceptually: echoes delayed by a few hundred milliseconds suggest a cathedral, while 10–20 ms delays suggest a modest room. [Chapter 1, Audio Processing]

Radar pulse length creates a clean engineering conflict—more energy extends detection range, but a longer pulse reduces range precision—then DSP pulse compression promises both. [Chapter 1, Echo Location]

The first CT scanner (1971) and the 1979 Hounsfield/Cormack Nobel Prize anchor tomography as a landmark DSP success that reconstructs cross-sectional images from many x-ray projections. [Chapter 1, Image Processing]

Random noise's practical peak-to-peak amplitude is about 6–8σ; the text dramatizes the Gaussian tail by noting that a >10σ event would be expected only for a few microseconds over roughly the age of the universe. [Chapter 2, The Normal Distribution]
The 'twelve uniforms' Gaussian generator is executable probability intuition: add twelve RND values, subtract six, then scale and shift. [Chapter 2, Digital Noise Generation, Fig. 2-10]

Dither's constant-voltage thought experiment is especially teachable: a true code of 3000.1 gives only 3000 without noise, but with dither about 90% of readings are 3000 and 10% are 3001, so 10,000 samples average near 3000.1. [Chapter 3, Quantization]

A 0.95-cycles/sample analog sine masquerades after sampling as a 0.05-cycles/sample sine—Smith's 'perfect crime' analogy for aliasing because the samples contain no clue to the original identity. [Chapter 3, The Sampling Theorem]

The 12-bit, 10 ksample/s antialias example shows why the top of a nominal Nyquist band is often unusable: an 8-pole Chebyshev must start its cutoff near 3.7 kHz to suppress content above 5 kHz. [Chapter 3, Analog Filters for Data Conversion]

The Mona Lisa line—viewers do not perceive an image as an 'interesting collection of sinusoids'—memorably separates time/space-domain encoding from audio's frequency-domain encoding and motivates different antialias priorities. [Chapter 3, Selecting the Antialias Filter]
A commercial delta-sigma ADC example operates its one-bit modulator at 6.4 MHz, uses a 246-tap FIR, and decimates 64:1 to deliver 16-bit samples at 100 kHz. [Chapter 3, Single-Bit Data Conversion]

The floating-loop bug prints 9.990133 and then skips the intended 10.00 endpoint; changing the control variable to an integer makes all 1,001 iterations exact. [Chapter 4, Number Precision, Table 4-2]

A lookup-table example maps each of 256 possible 8-bit voltage codes directly to resistor power; precomputation can be hundreds of times faster than evaluating P=V²/R repeatedly. [Chapter 4, Execution Speed: Programming Tips]

Aunt Edna's radish story and Uncle Bernie yelling at the dog emerge separately—not as 'Ednabernie'—to make additivity mean that superposed signals do not interact in a linear telephone system. [Chapter 5, Requirements for Linearity]

Multiplying 2041×4 by decomposing 2041 into 2000+40+1 is used as the everyday analogue of superposition: solve simple component problems and add the results. [Chapter 5, Superposition: the Foundation of DSP]

The convolution machine turns the index-heavy sum into a physical act: flip the impulse response, slide it, multiply aligned samples, and add, while the input-side story builds the same output from shifted impulse responses. [Chapter 6, The Input-Side Algorithm and The Output-Side Algorithm, Figs. 6-5–6-9]

A DC-removing high-pass convolution makes the first and last 30 output samples unusable, exposing edge effects as a practical consequence of incomplete data rather than a footnote about indexing. [Chapter 6, The Output-Side Algorithm, Fig. 6-10]

An intentionally irregular pulse looks strikingly Gaussian after only three self-convolutions, making the Central Limit Theorem visible as a signal operation. [Chapter 7, Mathematical Properties, Fig. 7-12]

Directly convolving one million samples with a 3,000-point impulse response is estimated at nearly an hour on the book's reference machine (and three days a decade earlier), a vivid setup for FFT convolution despite the dates of the hardware. [Chapter 7, Speed]

Fourier's 1807 claim that sinusoids represent periodic signals was rejected under Lagrange's objection about corners; the later resolution—arbitrarily close with zero-energy difference—previews the Gibbs effect. [Chapter 8, The Family of Fourier Transform]

The phase 'nuisance' checklist reads like a debugging guide: define π, use quadrant-aware arctangent, distrust phase where magnitude vanishes, unwrap 2π jumps, and recognize artificial π flips. [Chapter 8, Polar Nuisances]

The simulated undersea microphone spectrum encodes a detective story: a 13 Hz fundamental and harmonics could be a three-bladed propeller turning at 4.33 revolutions/s amid white noise, 1/f noise, 60 Hz hum, and antialias roll-off. [Chapter 9, Spectral Analysis of Signals, Fig. 9-2]

The 256-sample signal plus 51-sample kernel should produce 306 samples; forcing the calculation through a 256-point DFT wraps 50 tail samples into the front, making circular convolution literally visible. [Chapter 9, Convolution via the Frequency Domain, Fig. 9-9]

The phase chapter's central mnemonic is unusually durable: moving a waveform changes the slope of its phase but not its magnitude. The puzzling pulse centered at N/2 can legitimately be assigned three apparently different phase lines because π and 2π ambiguities make them equivalent. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase, Fig. 10-3]

Amplitude modulation makes negative frequency 'take human form': the negative-frequency copy of a 300 Hz–3 kHz voice spectrum becomes the physically transmitted lower sideband after shifting by the carrier. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation), Fig. 10-14]

The historical TV multiplexing ledger stacks eighty-two 6 MHz channels, from channel 3 at 60–66 MHz through channel 83 at 884–890 MHz, as a concrete example of frequency translation. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation)]

The 50-to-400-sample interpolation recipe is a ready-made lab: one smooth waveform interpolates gracefully, while an edge-rich waveform develops dramatic periodic ringing despite preserving exactly the original frequency content. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-13]

The sinc's zero crossings become intuitive through correlation: a rectangular pulse accumulates a sinusoid to zero whenever an integer number of cycles fits exactly inside its width. [Chapter 11, The Sinc Function]

Gibbs ringing supplies a striking limit experiment: more harmonics keep the overshoot near 9% while squeezing it to zero width, resolving the old objection that sinusoids cannot reconstruct a corner. [Chapter 11, Gibbs Effect, Fig. 11-6]
A nominal 1 kHz TTL square wave with nanosecond edges can carry harmonics nearly to 100 MHz—the ten-thousandth harmonic—making 'sharp edges require high frequencies' concrete. [Chapter 11, Harmonics]

Radar chirp compression resolves the conflict between range resolution and transmitter power: stretch energy into a long sweep for transmission, then use an antichirp to recover a narrow timing pulse. [Chapter 11, Chirp Signals]

The FFT is introduced with two memorable comparisons: its speedup is like flying rather than walking, and its foundational status in DSP is likened to the transistor in electronics. [Chapter 12, introduction and Further Speed Increases]

The 1024-point benchmark turns complexity into an unforgettable gap: about 25 seconds by direct correlation versus about 70 milliseconds by FFT on the reference machine. [Chapter 12, Speed and Precision Comparisons]

Mars and Sirius appear similarly point-like to the unaided eye even though their geometry differs enormously because both are impulses to the visual system; a telescope resolves Mars as a disk while Sirius remains a point-spread response. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function]

The chapter stretches 'impulse' across scales: a picosecond pulse can be impulsive to microwave electronics, while a years-long volcanic eruption can be impulsive relative to millennial geology. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function]

A one-resistor, one-capacitor circuit carries the whole continuous-systems story: its exponential impulse response is convolved region-by-region with a square pulse to derive charging and discharging without hiding the limits of integration. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Figs. 13-4–13-6]

A 1 kHz, 1 V pulse train at duty cycle 0.2 still reconstructs poorly with fourteen harmonics, making slow Fourier-series convergence and Gibbs overshoot visible in a concrete coefficient table. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series, Figs. 13-11–13-12]

Crystal oscillators top out near 10 MHz in the chapter's account, so a 150 MHz source is built by distorting a lower-frequency stable oscillator and isolating a selected harmonic with band-pass stages. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series]

The fetal-EKG example makes filter purpose explicit: a desired baby's heartbeat is mixed with the mother's breathing and heartbeat, so filtering is signal separation rather than merely smoothing. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics]

Smith's two-signal thought experiment—single solar-light samples carry event information, while no single wine-glass audio sample reveals its resonant frequency—cleanly separates time-encoded from frequency-encoded information. [Chapter 14, How Information Is Represented in Signals]

The moving average is defended against engineering embarrassment: its simplicity is not a compromise but the exact optimal equal-weight solution for white-noise reduction at fixed edge width. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response]

A 100-point moving average reduces random noise tenfold, yet recursive evaluation still needs only one addition and one subtraction per output after initialization. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response and Recursive Implementation]

A fiber-optic pulse naturally exits Gaussian-shaped because photons take different paths, tying repeated-convolution/Gaussian theory to a physical propagation effect. [Chapter 15, Relatives of the Moving Average Filter]

The EEG design turns abstract passbands into physiology: eyes-closed alpha activity occupies about 7–12 Hz, eyes-open beta about 17–20 Hz, and a 101-point filter at 100 samples/s separates them. [Chapter 16, Examples of Windowed-Sinc Filters]

The extreme windowed-sinc example asks for a 1 mV signal riding on a 120 V power line, motivating at least −120 dB attenuation and then obtaining about −148 dB by filtering twice. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit]

A 32,001-point FIR is specified to pass DC–1000 Hz within 0.02% and reject everything above 1001 Hz to below 0.02%, dramatizing how long kernels buy narrow transitions. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit, Fig. 16-7]

Gamma-ray pulse pile-up makes deconvolution tangible: sodium-iodide scintillation decays over hundreds of nanoseconds, overlapping events corrupt energy estimates, and inverse filtering narrows the pulses until noise/model error sets the limit. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Figs. 17-3–17-5]

The deconvolution chapter's blunt information limit is pedagogically useful: once an attenuated frequency falls below noise—or is reduced to zero—no processing can recover it; inverse gain only amplifies ignorance. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution]

Restoring Enrico Caruso recordings becomes a historical blind-deconvolution case: unknown horn resonances are estimated by comparing averaged spectra of old recordings with modern performances and then counter-equalized. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Fig. 17-6]

The three 'optimal' filters produce visually unimpressive differences, which Smith uses to teach a broader lesson: optimizing one metric does not automatically optimize the human task or justify added complexity. [Chapter 17, Optimal Filters, Fig. 17-9]

The 10-million-sample FFT-convolution example is a complete bookkeeping set piece: 16,000 blocks ×625 samples, a 400-point kernel, 1024-point FFTs, 399 saved overlap samples, and exactly 10,000,399 outputs. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Table 18-1]

For long kernels, cost becomes surprisingly flat: a 16,000-point FFT-convolution kernel takes only about twice the execution time of a 64-point one in the chapter's rule-of-thumb comparison. [Chapter 18, Speed Improvements]
The vanished-professor story asks what information remained available to calculate y[28], making feedback recursion feel inevitable rather than formal. [Chapter 19, The Recursive Method, Fig. 19-1]

A one-pole filter with x=0.86 has a 6.63-sample time constant; the number turns an abstract feedback coefficient into visible exponential memory. [Chapter 19, Single Pole Recursive Filters, Eq. 19-4 and Fig. 19-3]

Forward-plus-reverse filtering earns Smith's theatrical 'Voila!' and a backwards warning sentence, a memorable reveal that exact zero phase costs only a second pass. [Chapter 19, Phase Response, Fig. 19-8]

Smith offers two definitions of a pole: roots of a complex denominator, or containers of magic powder—the more poles, the better the filter. The joke cleanly separates usage from derivation. [Chapter 20, Designing the Filter]

The unstable 6-pole, fc=0.01 coefficient set makes the numerical problem visceral: a coefficients near 10^-9 are overwhelmed by round-off in b coefficients near ten. [Chapter 20, Stability, Table 20-1]

The filter-comparison chapter stages three literal prize fights and reaches a crisp maxim: the windowed-sinc is a powerhouse, the Chebyshev is quick and agile. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev]

A maximum-performance thought experiment asks for a 100 mV, 61 Hz signal riding on a 120 V, 60 Hz power line; the 1001-tap FIR crushes the 6-pole IIR if one can wait. [Chapter 21, Match #2: Windowed-Sinc vs. Chebyshev, Fig. 21-4]

The ear's dynamic range reaches roughly one million in amplitude, yet the eardrum moves less than a molecule's diameter at threshold and listeners perceive only about 120 loudness increments. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing, Table 22-1]
Covering 99% of a wall with perfect soundproofing still leaves perceived loudness near 20%, because loudness scales roughly as sound power to the one-third power. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing]

A 3-degree directional discrimination corresponds to roughly 30 microseconds of interaural delay for a 22 cm head—an arresting bridge from perception to sampling-scale timing. [Chapter 22, Human Hearing]
Two dramatically different 1 kHz ± 3 kHz waveforms sound the same, showing why waveform shape is not a one-to-one description of timbre. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Fig. 22-2]
The piano spans only about 20% of the linear 20 kHz hearing range but more than 70% of perceptual information because it covers seven of roughly ten audible octaves. [Chapter 22, Timbre, Fig. 22-4]

CD's physical story connects 0.8-3.5 μm pits, EFM's 8-to-14 mapping, Reed-Solomon protection, 4.3 Mbit/s raw storage, and 706 kbit/s recovered audio in one chain. [Chapter 22, High Fidelity Audio, Figs. 22-5 and 22-6]
The paired phrases 'spider ring' and 'spy during' illustrate why acoustic word matching without context is not speech understanding. [Chapter 22, Speech Synthesis and Recognition]
Homomorphic jargon literally swaps pieces of words—cepstrum, quefrency, liftering—because time and frequency roles have been reversed. [Chapter 22, Nonlinear Audio Processing, Fig. 22-12]
A 200x200 radar image of Venus is peeled into a 16x16 pixel patch and then into its exact numbers, making 'image as array' concrete. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure, Fig. 23-1]
One second of Smith-era digital audio is about 8 kB while one second of television is about 8 MB; a 1000x1000 image quadruples the burden of 500x500. [Chapter 23, Digital Image Structure]

The infrared intruder/truck example shows manual grayscale design making background and grille details visible at the explicit expense of the human body's contrast. [Chapter 23, Grayscale Transforms, Figs. 23-13 and 23-14]
Mach bands turn the retina's useful edge enhancement into an illusion: the dark side looks darker and the light side lighter near a gradual boundary. [Chapter 24, Convolution, Figs. 24-1 and 24-2]

A 512x512 image convolved with a 64x64 PSF needs more than a billion multiply-adds, motivating 3x3 kernels, separability, and FFT convolution as three distinct escape routes. [Chapter 24, Convolution]

The Gaussian is uniquely both circularly symmetric and separable; broad rectangular or exponential kernels can go further and make cost independent of kernel width. [Chapter 24, Convolution by Separability, Fig. 24-7]

A line-pair gauge slightly overstates resolution because its square-wave fundamental is 4/π ≈ 1.27 times the square-wave amplitude—an often ignored measurement wrinkle. [Chapter 25, Spatial Resolution, Fig. 25-2]

Doubling an object's diameter lets it be detected in roughly twice as much noise, because matched spatial averaging makes detectability scale with the square root of area. [Chapter 25, Signal-to-Noise Ratio, Fig. 25-8]

The 1972 EMI Mark I used ART, while filtered backprojection later became dominant; the chapter turns that history into a progression from iterative correction to exact DSP reconstruction. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-15 through 25-17]
The Fourier-slice 'wheel spokes are denser near the hub' analogy makes the ramp filter H(f)=|f| almost visually inevitable. [Chapter 25, Computed Tomography, Figs. 25-18 and 25-19]

The rare-cancer example demonstrates base-rate neglect numerically: identical instrument output can suggest 25% disease probability or only 0.025% once prevalence is included. [Chapter 26, Target Detection, Fig. 26-1]

Smith's paratrooper dropped into a foggy mountain valley compares blind random evolution with measuring north/east slopes and walking downhill—the chapter's central steepest-descent analogy. [Chapter 26, Training the Neural Network, Fig. 26-9]

The best handwritten-vowel network detects 24 of 25 vowels with one false alarm per 25 nonvowels, despite hidden-layer weights that look like random noise to a person. [Chapter 26, Evaluating the Results, Figs. 26-10 through 26-12]

The same iterative machinery used to train a neural network designs a custom recursive filter, joining apparently different topics through the shared idea of optimizing many parameters. [Chapter 26, Recursive Filter Design, Fig. 26-13]

A 1990s web-download calculation makes compression tangible: a roughly 600-kbyte photograph over a 33.6-kbps modem takes about 142 seconds uncompressed, 71 seconds after lossless compression, and 12 seconds as a roughly 50-kbyte JPEG. [Chapter 27, Data Compression Strategies, printed p. 482]

The Huffman text histogram finds that more than 96% of a chapter consists of only 31 characters; a simple five-bit/common-character scheme averages 5.32 bits per character for about 1.5:1 compression. [Chapter 27, Huffman Encoding, Fig. 27-2]

The LZW algorithm is traced byte by byte through the phrase 'the/rain/in/Spain/falls/mainly/on/the/plain,' showing exactly when dictionary strings are added and emitted. [Chapter 27, LZW Compression, Table 27-3]

The JPEG eye block remains recognizable with only 15 of 64 DCT coefficients, while the full photograph at 45:1 compression makes each 8×8 block average fewer than 12 stored bits and visibly reveals the grid. [Chapter 27, JPEG, Figs. 27-12 and 27-15]

MPEG is taught as both compression and editing structure: independently coded I-pictures provide random access, P-pictures exploit temporal redundancy, and B-pictures look both backward and forward. [Chapter 27, MPEG, printed p. 502]

The FIR implementation inventory lists fourteen recurring actions and then shows that a DSP can execute loop steps 6–12 in one clock cycle by parallelizing multiply, add, two fetches, pointer updates, and loop control. [Chapter 28, Circular Buffering and Architecture, Table 28-1]

The benchmark warning is memorable: choosing a processor from a single MIPS/MFLOPS number is compared with asking whether a Cadillac or Ferrari is the better car—the answer depends on the job. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

A 1024-point complex FFT on the historical 40-MHz ADSP-21062 is budgeted at 18,221 cycles (about 0.46 ms), and the chapter converts that marketing-style fact into the reusable metric of 17.8 cycles/sample. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]

The direct-versus-FFT convolution crossover is worked end to end: a 512-sample block, zero-padding to 1024, forward/inverse FFTs, overlap-add, about 60 cycles/sample, and a roughly 60-tap break-even point. [Chapter 28, How Fast Are DSPs?]
A memory-sizing sanity check translates 544 kbits into 6–8 seconds of 8-kHz, 8-bit speech and 4 Mbits into one 512×512 8-bit image. [Chapter 29, The ADSP-2106x Family, Table 29-1]

The 301-tap FIR assembly listing makes architecture visible: two circular memories feed a multiply, prior product is accumulated, and the next pair is fetched—all on one loop line. [Chapter 29, Design Example: An FIR Audio Filter, Table 29-2]

The analog-engineer vignette turns exact linear phase into a surprise: a 301-point symmetric kernel delays every feature by 150 samples, so the oscilloscope appears mis-triggered even though the system is behaving perfectly. [Chapter 29, Analog Measurements on a DSP System]

The measured-response experiment steps a generator from 125 Hz to 10 kHz in 125-Hz increments and finds the hardware points tracking the intentionally irregular theoretical FIR curve within measurement error. [Chapter 29, Fig. 29-4]

The complex-substitution counterexample uses apple prices and orange prices to show why merely packing two real quantities into a+jb does not guarantee that complex multiplication preserves the original physical problem. [Chapter 30, Using Complex Numbers by Substitution]

A sinusoid is followed across three equivalent languages—ordinary amplitude/phase, rectangular cosine/sine coefficients, and one complex number—then through a system whose complex gain halves amplitude and shifts phase by 3π/8. [Chapter 30, Complex Representation of Systems, Fig. 30-4]

The Laplace train analogy distinguishes exhaustive samples from causal structure: the passenger records every elevation, while the conductor summarizes the route as a mountain, valley, and overall rise—like poles and zeros compressing a full response. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform]

Five probe waveforms against one notch-filter impulse response turn abstract poles, zeros, and region of convergence into cancellation, finite area, and runaway area. [Chapter 32, Strategy of the Laplace Transform, Fig. 32-5]

The Sallen-Key gain sweep is a compact stability drama: gain 1 yields two real poles, 1.586 places them at 45 degrees, 2.5 produces peaking, and gain 3 reaches the imaginary axis and turns the filter into an oscillator. [Chapter 32, Filter Design in the s-Domain, Fig. 32-9]

The z-plane is explained by an ant walking the unit circle and evaluating H(z) at about 1000 points; the text then undercuts the ideal plot by warning that implemented coefficients can still be unstable, motivating impulse-and-FFT verification. [Chapter 33, Analysis of Recursive Systems]

Recursive spectral inversion is a useful failure case: subtracting a sixth-order Butterworth low-pass from the input produces a terrible high-pass because phase blocks cancellation, whereas notch-to-band-pass inversion fares somewhat better. [Chapter 33, Spectral Inversion, Fig. 33-6]

Benford's origin story begins with the visibly worn first pages of logarithm tables and expands to more than 20,000 values collected from atomic weights, magazine numbers, baseball statistics, and river areas. [Chapter 34, Frank Benford's Discovery]

The empirical confrontation uses 14,414 corporate-tax values against a Gaussian RNG: the tax data show 30.1% leading ones while the RNG does not, immediately posing both the law and its exceptions. [Chapter 34, Fig. 34-2]

The Ones Scaling Test runs 696 multiplications by 1.01, spanning about three orders of magnitude, and repeats every 232 steps because multiplying by ten preserves the leading digit. [Chapter 34, The Ones Scaling Test, Fig. 34-3 and Table 34-1]

A sharp quantitative transition makes the mystery memorable: changing a log-normal distribution's 2σ width from 0.5 to 1.0 changes the predicted leading-one swing from 16–45% to under 1%. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, Fig. 34-8]

The book estimates that a log-normal with σ=3 misses exact Benford compliance by such a tiny finite amount that even a billion computers generating a billion numbers per second since the universe began could not statistically expose it. [Chapter 34, Analysis of the Log-Normal Distribution, printed p. 720]

The final application closes the loop from theory to practice: fabricated financial numbers are unlikely to preserve the broad log-domain structure, so leading-digit deviations can flag reports for forensic scrutiny. [Chapter 34, The Power of Signal Processing]
